nodes.name: weighted graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{(finite, undirected) weighted graph} $G$ is a quadruple $(V,E,\mu,w)$ with a \emph{vertex set} $V=\{1,\cdots,n\}$, an \emph{edge set} \[E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\text{ in }V\},\] a \emph{vertex weight} $\mu:V\to \mathbb{R}^+$, and an \emph{edge weight} $w:E\to \mathbb{R}^+$.
nodes.statement_short: A weighted graph is $(V,E,\mu,w)$ with vertex set, edge set, positive vertex weights and positive edge weights.

nodes.name: edge and vertex weight notation
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we use $w_{uv}$ and $\mu_v$ to denote $w(\{u,v\})$ and $\mu(v)$, respectively.

nodes.name: boundary of a vertex set
nodes.statement: For any subset $A\subseteq V$ of vertices, define the \emph{boundary} $\partial A$ of $A$ by \[\partial A:=\{\{u,v\}\in E\colon u\in A, v\not\in A\}.\]

nodes.name: Cheeger k-constant
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{Cheeger $k$-constant} of $G$ by \[h_k(G):=\min_{\text{subpartitions }(A_1,\dots,A_k)\text{ of }V}~\max_{1\le i\le k}\phi(A_i),\] where \[\phi(A_i):=\phi_{\mu,w}(A_i):=\frac{w(\partial A)}{\mu(A)}:=\frac{\sum\limits_{\{u,v\}\in\partial A}w_{uv}}{\sum\limits_{v\in A}\mu_v}\] is the \textsl{expansion} (Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan, \cite{Lee-Gharan-Trevisan}) of $A_i$, and by $(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ being a \emph{subpartition} of $V$ we mean that $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: $h_k(G)$ is the minimum over $k$-subpartitions of the maximal expansion $\phi(A_i)=w(\partial A_i)/\mu(A_i)$.

nodes.name: k-th min-max eigenvalue of the graph p-Laplacian
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_{k}(\Delta_p)$ denote the $k$-th min-max eigenvalue of the graph $p$-Laplacian $\Delta_p$, where the relevant concepts and terminology are detailed in Section \ref{sec:minmax-eigen-1-Lap}.

nodes.name: normalized graph Laplacian
nodes.statement: When $p=2$, $\Delta_2$ is called the \emph{(normalized) graph Laplacian}, and $\lambda_{k}(\Delta_2)$ is the $k$-th smallest eigenvalue of $\Delta_2$.

nodes.name: Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan higher-order Cheeger inequality
nodes.statement: Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan \cite{Lee-Gharan-Trevisan}: There exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that $$\frac{1}{Ck^4}h_k(G)^2\le\lambda_k(\Delta_2)\le2h_k(G).$$
nodes.statement_short: $h_k^2/(Ck^4)\le\lambda_k(\Delta_2)\le 2h_k$ for a universal constant $C$.
conclusions: There exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that $$\frac{1}{Ck^4}h_k(G)^2\le\lambda_k(\Delta_2)\le2h_k(G).$$

nodes.name: Tudisco-Hein higher-order Cheeger inequality for the graph p-Laplacian
nodes.statement: Tudisco-Hein \cite{Tudisco}: For $p>1$, let $x$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_k(\Delta_p)$, and assume that $x$ has $m$ strong nodal domains. Then, $$ \frac{2^{p-1}}{p^p}h_m(G)^p\le\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le 2^{p-1}h_k(G).$$
nodes.statement_short: If an eigenvector of $\lambda_k(\Delta_p)$ has $m$ strong nodal domains, then $\frac{2^{p-1}}{p^p}h_m^p\le\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le 2^{p-1}h_k$.
assumptions: let $x$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_k(\Delta_p)$
assume that $x$ has $m$ strong nodal domains

nodes.name: Daneshgar-Javadi-Miclo Cheeger inequality on trees
nodes.statement: Daneshgar-Javadi-Miclo \cite{Daneshgar,Miclo}: For any simple tree, $$\frac{1}{2}h_k(G)^2\le \lambda_{k}(\Delta_2)\le 2 h_k(G).$$

nodes.name: Deidda-Putti-Tudisco 1-Laplacian Cheeger identity on trees
nodes.statement: Deidda-Putti-Tudisco \cite{Deidda}: For any weighted tree, $$\lambda_{k}(\Delta_1)= h_k(G).$$

nodes.name: Courant-Fischer-Weyl minimax principle
nodes.statement: For any symmetric matrix $\mathbf{A}\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, the $k$-th smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_k(\mathbf{A})$ can be written as $$ \lambda_k(\mathbf{A})=\min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X\ge k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x} = \max_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X\ge n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The $k$-th smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix is a min-max and a max-min of the Rayleigh quotient over subspaces.
conclusions: the $k$-th smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_k(\mathbf{A})$ can be written as $$ \lambda_k(\mathbf{A})=\min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X\ge k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x} = \max_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X\ge n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x}.$$

nodes.name: min-max = max-min equality for the Rayleigh quotient
nodes.statement: \min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x} = \max_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{x^\top \mathbf{A} x}{x^\top x},
nodes.statement_short: Min over $k$-dim subspaces of max Rayleigh quotient equals max over $(n-k+1)$-dim subspaces of min.
nodes.label: eq:minmax=maxmin-Courant

nodes.name: combinatorial Courant-Fischer-Weyl minimax principle
nodes.statement: For any forest $G=(V,E,\mu,w)$, we have \[\min_{\mathrm{subpartitions~}(A_1,\dots,A_{k})\mathrm{~of~}V}~~\max_{B\in \mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_{k})}\phi(B)=\max_{\mathrm{subpartitions~}(A_1,\dots,A_{n-k+1})\mathrm{~of~}V}~~\min_{B\in \mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_{n-k+1})}\phi(B),\] where \[\mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_k)=\{A_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{i_q}:1\le i_1<\cdots<i_q\le k,\,1\le q\le k\}\] denotes the union-closed family generated by the subpartition $(A_1,\dots,A_{k})$ of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: On a forest, the min-max of $\phi$ over union-closed families of $k$-subpartitions equals the max-min over $(n-k+1)$-subpartitions.
nodes.label: thm:CombinatorialCourant-Fischer

nodes.name: Courant-Fischer-Weyl minimax principle for graph Laplacian
nodes.statement: \min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}(x_u-x_v)^2}{\sum\limits_v\mu_vx_v^2} = \max_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}(x_u-x_v)^2}{\sum\limits_v\mu_vx_v^2},
nodes.statement_short: Min-max over $k$-dim subspaces of the graph Rayleigh quotient equals the max-min over $(n-k+1)$-dim subspaces.
conclusions: \min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}(x_u-x_v)^2}{\sum\limits_v\mu_vx_v^2} = \max_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}(x_u-x_v)^2}{\sum\limits_v\mu_vx_v^2},
nodes.label: eq:classical-minmax-Lap

nodes.name: nonlinear Courant-Fischer-Weyl minimax principle
nodes.statement: For any forest, \begin{align*}\min_{\substack{\mathrm{linear~subspaces~}X\mathrm{~of~}\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} = \max_{\substack{\mathrm{linear~subspaces~}X\mathrm{~of~}\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: On a forest, min-max and max-min of the $L^1$ Rayleigh quotient over subspaces of dimension $k$ and $n-k+1$ coincide.
conclusions: \begin{align*}\min_{\substack{\mathrm{linear~subspaces~}X\mathrm{~of~}\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} = \max_{\substack{\mathrm{linear~subspaces~}X\mathrm{~of~}\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:nonlinearCourant-Fischer

nodes.name: both minimax equalities equal the Cheeger k-constant on forests
nodes.statement: It is noteworthy that both equalities in Theorem \ref{thm:CombinatorialCourant-Fischer} and Theorem \ref{thm:nonlinearCourant-Fischer} are equal to $h_k(G)$ when $G$ is a forest.
conclusions: both equalities in Theorem \ref{thm:CombinatorialCourant-Fischer} and Theorem \ref{thm:nonlinearCourant-Fischer} are equal to $h_k(G)$

nodes.name: set of k-subpartitions
nodes.statement: Let \[\mathcal{P}_k(V):=\{(A_1,\dots,A_{k}):~\varnothing\ne A_i\subseteq V,\,A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\,\forall i\ne j\}\] be the set of all subpartitions of $V$ with $k$ subsets.

nodes.name: union-closed reformulation of the Cheeger k-constant
nodes.statement: For any weighted graph $G=(V,E,\mu,w)$, $$h_k(G):=\min_{(A_1,\dots,A_{k})\in \mathcal{P}_k(V)}~\max_{1\le i\le k}\phi(A_i)=\min_{(A_1,\dots,A_{k})\in \mathcal{P}_k(V)}~\max_{B\in \mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_{k})}\phi(B)$$ where \[\mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_k):=\{A_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{i_q}:1\le i_1<\cdots<i_q\le k,\,1\le q\le k\}\] stands for the union closed family generated by the $k$-tuple of sets $(A_1,\cdots,A_k)$.
nodes.statement_short: $h_k$ is unchanged when the max over the $k$ sets is replaced by the max over all their unions.
nodes.label: prop:unioninv

nodes.name: max-min Cheeger constant, Dirichlet Cheeger constant and Cheeger constant of a set
nodes.statement: For any weighted graph $G=(V,E,\mu,w)$ with $n$ vertices, let $$\ell_k(G):=\max_{(A_1,\dots,A_{n-k+1})\in \mathcal{P}_{n-k+1}(V)}~\min_{B\in \mathcal{U}(A_1,\cdots,A_{n-k+1})}\phi(B)$$ be the $k$-th max-min Cheeger constant, and let $$\underline{\ell_k}(G) :=\max_{A\subseteq V,~|A|=n-k+1}h(A)$$ be the $k$-th Dirichlet Cheeger constant \cite{DTZ}, where \[h(A):=\min_{B\subseteq A}\phi(B)\] denotes the Cheeger constant of $A$ with respect to $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_k$: max over $(n-k+1)$-subpartitions of min $\phi$ over unions; $\underline{\ell_k}$: max of $h(A)$ over $|A|=n-k+1$; $h(A)=\min_{B\subseteq A}\phi(B)$.

nodes.name: max-min characterization of Cheeger k-constants of weighted forests
nodes.statement: For any weighted graph $\tilde G=(\tilde V,\tilde E,\tilde\mu,\tilde w)$ with $n$ vertices, for any $k\in\{1,2,\cdots,n\}$, we have \[h_k(\tilde G)\ge \ell_k(\tilde G)\ge \underline{\ell_k}(\tilde G).\] For any weighted forest $G=(V,E,\mu,w)$ with $n$ vertices, we must have \[h_k(G)= \ell_k(G)= \underline{\ell_k}(G).\]
nodes.statement_short: $h_k\ge\ell_k\ge\underline{\ell_k}$ on every weighted graph, with equality throughout on weighted forests.

nodes.name: Cheeger constant inequality with number of independent loops
nodes.statement: For any weighted graph $\tilde G=(\tilde V,\tilde E,\tilde\mu,\tilde w)$, \[h_k(\tilde G)\ge \ell_k(\tilde G)\ge \underline{\ell_k}(\tilde G)\ge h_{k-\beta}(\tilde G),\] where $\beta:=|\tilde E|-|\tilde V|+c$ is the total number of independent loops of $\tilde G$, and $c$ is the number of connected components of $\tilde G$.
nodes.statement_short: On any graph, $h_k\ge\ell_k\ge\underline{\ell_k}\ge h_{k-\beta}$ where $\beta$ is the number of independent loops.

nodes.name: variational min-max eigenvalue of the p-Laplacian with an index
nodes.statement: All of them are obtained by a \emph{minimax} procedure: \begin{equation} \lambda_k^{\mathrm{ind}}(\Delta_p):=\inf_{\substack{S\text{ origin-symmetric, compact}\\\mathrm{ind}(S)\ge k}}~\sup_{f\in S}\frac{\int_\Omega|\nabla f(z)|^pdz}{\int_\Omega|f(z)|^pdz} \end{equation} where $\mathrm{ind}(\cdot)$ is an admissible index for origin-symmetric compact subsets of the Sobolev space $H_0^1(\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Krasnoselskii genus
nodes.statement: Krasnoselskii genus: The \emph{Krasnoselskii genus} of an origin-symmetric compact set $S$ is defined by $$\gamma(S):=\min\{k\in\mathbb{Z}^+:\exists\text{ odd continuous }\varphi:S\to \mathbb{R}^k\setminus\{0\}\}.$$

nodes.name: Conner-Floyd index
nodes.statement: Conner-Floyd index: The \emph{Conner-Floyd index} $\gamma^+$ of an origin-symmetric compact set $S$ is defined by $$\gamma^+(S):=\min\{k\in\mathbb{Z}^+:\exists\text{ odd continuous }\varphi:\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\to S\setminus\{0\}\},$$ where $\mathbb{S}^{k-1}$ stands for the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^k$.

nodes.name: Drabek-Robinson eigenvalues
nodes.statement: The min-max eigenvalues of $p$-Laplacian using $\mathrm{ind}=\gamma^+$ are called the Drabek-Robinson eigenvalues \cite{Drabek}.

nodes.name: Yang index
nodes.statement: Yang index: This index, denoted by $\textrm{Y-ind}(\cdot)$, is defined via homology information \cite{Yang}.

nodes.name: admissible index
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of all origin-symmetric compact subsets. An index $\mathrm{ind}:\mathcal{S}\to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ is \emph{admissible} if it satisfies the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $\mathrm{ind}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})=k$, where $k=1,2,\cdots$ \item[(2)] monotonicity: If $A\subseteq A'$, then $$\mathrm{ind}(S)\le \mathrm{ind}(S').$$ \item[(3)] continuity: For any $S$, there exists a closed neighborhood $U$ of $S$ such that $$\mathrm{ind}(U)= \mathrm{ind}(S).$$ \item[(4)] nondecreasing under odd continuous map: For any odd continuous map $\eta$, $$\mathrm{ind}(S)\le \mathrm{ind}(\eta(S)).$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.1 Applications on min-max eigenvalues of Graph 1-Laplacian of Forests
nodes.statement_short: An index on origin-symmetric compact sets is admissible if it is normalized on spheres, monotone, continuous and nondecreasing under odd maps.

nodes.name: variational min-max values with an admissible index are eigenvalues
nodes.statement: By the standard approach in defining variational min-max eigenvalues of $\Delta_p$, we state that for every $k$, $\lambda_k^{\mathrm{ind}}(\Delta_p)$ defined with an admissible index must be an eigenvalue of $\Delta_p$ (see \cite{DTZ,Zhang}).
nodes.section: 2.1 Applications on min-max eigenvalues of Graph 1-Laplacian of Forests
conclusions: $\lambda_k^{\mathrm{ind}}(\Delta_p)$ defined with an admissible index must be an eigenvalue of $\Delta_p$

nodes.name: Krasnoselskii and Conner-Floyd eigenvalues agree for k=1,2
nodes.statement: It is known that $\lambda_1^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)= \lambda_1^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$, $\lambda_2^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)= \lambda_2^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$ and $\lambda_k^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)\le \lambda_k^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$ for general $k$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Applications on min-max eigenvalues of Graph 1-Laplacian of Forests
conclusions: It is known that $\lambda_1^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)= \lambda_1^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$, $\lambda_2^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)= \lambda_2^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$ and $\lambda_k^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)\le \lambda_k^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$ for general $k$.

nodes.statement: However, the fundamental question of whether the general equality $\lambda_k^{\gamma}(\Delta_p)= \lambda_k^{\gamma^+}(\Delta_p)$ holds for every $k$ remains unresolved.

nodes.name: tightness of the refined Cheeger inequality as p tends to 1
nodes.statement: We can rewrite the inequality in {Corollary \ref{cor:tree-p-Lap}} as $$ \swarrow\frac{1}{2^{p-1}}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le h_k(G)\le \frac p2 (2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}\nearrow. $$ Then, by the increasing property of $\frac p2 (2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}$ with respect to $p\in[1,+\infty)$, and the decreasing property of $\frac{1}{2^{p-1}}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)$ with respect to $p\in[1,+\infty)$, the inequality becomes tight when $p$ tends to 1.

nodes.name: nonadjacent sets

nodes.name: expansion of a disjoint union
nodes.statement: For any disjoint subsets $A$ and $B$ of $V$, we have $\phi(A\cup B)\le \max\left\{\phi(A),\phi(B)\right\}$. If we further assume that $E(A,B)=\varnothing$, then we have $$\min\left\{\phi(A),\phi(B)\right\} \le \phi(A\cup B)\le \max\left\{\phi(A),\phi(B)\right\}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Let $a=w(\partial A)$, $b=\mu(A)$, $c=w(\partial B)$, $d=\mu(B)$. Then \[w(\partial(A\cup B))\le a+c\text{ and }\mu(A\cup B)=b+d,\] so $\phi(A\cup B)\le\frac{a+c}{b+d}$. Now suppose for the sake of contradiction that \[\frac ab<\frac{a+c}{b+d}\text{ and }\frac cd<\frac{a+c}{b+d},\] then summing up yields \[\frac{ad+bc}{bd}<\frac{a+c}{b+d}\iff ad^2+b^2c<0,\] which is a contradiction, so it follows that $\phi(A\cup B)\le\max\{\phi(A),\phi(B)\}$. If in addition $E(A,B)=\varnothing$, then $w(\partial(A\cup B))=a+c$ and $\phi(A\cup B)=\frac{a+c}{b+d}$, so the remaining inequality follows similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\phi$ as ratios $a/b$, $c/d$; assuming both are below the mediant gives $ad^2+b^2c<0$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Cheeger constant of a union of subpartition sets
nodes.statement: For any subpartition $(B_1,\cdots,B_k)$ of $V$, we have \[h(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k)\le \min\{h(B_1),\cdots,h(B_k)\}.\] If we further assume that $E(B_i,B_j)=\varnothing$ whenever $i\ne j$, then we have \[h(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k)=\min\{h(B_1),\cdots,h(B_k)\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: $h$ of a union is at most the min of the $h(B_i)$, with equality when the $B_i$ are pairwise nonadjacent.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Suppose $C\subseteq B_1\cup\dots\cup B_k$ is such that $\phi(C)=h(B_1\cup\dots\cup B_k)$, then we can assume that $C$ is connected, because otherwise we can replace $C$ by one of its connected components that possesses the minimum $\phi$-value without affecting the minimality by Lemma \ref{lemma:basic-phi}, so $C\subseteq B_j$ for some $1\le j\le k$. Thus, \[\phi(C)=h(B_j)=\min\{h(B_1),\dots,h(B_k)\},\] this concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimizer $C$, reduce to a connected one by Lemma 1, which then lies in a single $B_j$.

nodes.name: common union of two subpartitions (pigeonhole lemma)
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Suppose that \[(A_1,\dots,A_k)\text{ and }(B_1,\dots,B_{n-k+1})\] are subpartitions of $[n]:=\{1,\dots, n\}$, then there exists a nonempty subset $\{i_1,\dots,i_t\}$ of $[k]$ and a nonempty subset $\{j_1,\dots,j_s\}$ of $[n-k+1]$ such that \[A_{i_1}\cup\dots\cup A_{i_t}=B_{j_1}\cup\dots\cup B_{j_s}.\]
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-subpartition and an $(n-k+1)$-subpartition of $[n]$ always share a nonempty common union of parts.
assumptions: Suppose that \[(A_1,\dots,A_k)\text{ and }(B_1,\dots,B_{n-k+1})\] are subpartitions of $[n]:=\{1,\dots, n\}$
conclusions: there exists a nonempty subset $\{i_1,\dots,i_t\}$ of $[k]$ and a nonempty subset $\{j_1,\dots,j_s\}$ of $[n-k+1]$ such that \[A_{i_1}\cup\dots\cup A_{i_t}=B_{j_1}\cup\dots\cup B_{j_s}.\]
nodes.label: lem:pigeonhole

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: We apply strong induction on $n$. The base case $n=1$ is obvious. In general, if $(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ and $(B_1,\dots,B_{n-k+1})$ are partitions of $[n]$, then we are done. Otherwise, let \[C=\left(\bigcup_{1\le i\le k} A_i\right)\bigcap\left(\bigcup_{1\le j\le n-k+1} B_j\right),\] then we have $c:=|C|<n$. Note that at most $n-c$ subsets among the $A_i$'s and the $B_j$'s contain elements outside $C$. In other words, at least $c+1$ subsets contain only elements in $C$. Now we apply the induction hypothesis on $C$ and the two subpartitions formed by those at least $c+1$ subsets.
nodes.statement_short: Strong induction on $n$: if not partitions, restrict to the common support $C$, where at least $|C|+1$ parts live, and induct.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: The proposition follows immediately from Lemma \ref{lem:cheeger-set-disjoint}, which implies that choosing from $\mathcal U(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ will not make it strictly larger than choosing from $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma 2: unions never have smaller-than-min Cheeger value, so allowing unions does not increase the max.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Choose an extremal $k$-subpartition (min max-$\phi$, then fewest maximizers, then least weight); its sets are connected, and deleting $k-1$ vertices of a tree makes them nonadjacent, giving $\underline{\ell_k}\ge h_k$. The reverse $h_k\ge\ell_k$ uses the pigeonhole lemma.

nodes.name: Proof divided into steps
nodes.statement: Due to its overwhelming length, we divide our proof into several steps.
nodes.statement_short: Proof divided into steps

nodes.name: Step 1: extremal subpartition
nodes.statement: \underline{Step 1. Setup.} \newline\noindent For ease of presentation, we prove the case when $G$ is a weighted tree, whereas the proof for the general case of weighted forests is done by mimicking the following proof. Let \[S_1:=arg\,min_{\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in\mathcal{P}_k(V)}~\max_{1\le i\le k}\phi(A_i)\] be the set of all subpartitions that minimize the maximum $\phi$-value among the subsets. For reasons that will become clear later, we do not attempt to start working on a subpartition in $S_1$. Instead, we need more requirements on the subpartitions than that and furthur refine our desired class by letting \[S_2:=arg\,min_{\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in S_1}f(\mathcal A),\] where \[f(\mathcal A)=|\{1\le i\le k\colon\phi(A_i)=h_k\}|,\] be the set of all subpartitions in $S_1$ minimizing the number of subsets sharing the maximum $\phi$-value and \[S_3:=arg\,min_{\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in S_2}~\sum_{i=1}^k\mu(A_i)\] be the set of all subpartitions in $S_2$ that minimize the total weighted degree. Now, pick any subpartition $\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in S_3$. By reordering if necessary, suppose that \[\phi(A_1)\le\dots\le\phi(A_k)=h_k\] without loss of generality.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to trees; pick a subpartition minimizing max-$\phi$, then the number of maximizers, then total weight.

nodes.name: Step 2: achieving pairwise nonadjacency
nodes.statement: \underline{Step 2. Achieving pairwise nonadjacency.} \newline\noindent We prove that there exists $v_1\in A_1,\dots,v_{k-1}\in A_{k-1}$ such that \[A_1\setminus\{v_1\},\dots,A_{k-1}\setminus\{v_{k-1}\},V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1})\] are pairwise nonadjacent in this step. Indeed, since $\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in S_3$, each $A_i$ is connected. (This is because otherwise, if some $A_j$ is not connected, then we write \[A_j=A_{j1}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm},\] where $A_{j1},\dots,A_{jm}$ are the $m$ connected components of $A_j$. Now, by Lemma \ref{lemma:basic-phi}, since \[E(A_{j1},A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm})=\varnothing,\] we have \[\min\{\phi(A_{j1}),\phi(A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm})\}\le\phi(A_j).\] If it happens that $\phi(A_{j1})>\phi(A_j)$, then we apply Lemma \ref{lemma:basic-phi} and the same procedure on \[A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm}=A_{j2}\cup(A_{j3}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm}),\] and eventually we will obtain some $1\le p\le m$ such that $\phi(A_{jp})\le\phi(A_j)$. Now note that the subpartition \[\tilde{\mathcal A}=(A_1,\dots,A_{jp},\dots,A_k)\] is in $S_1$, since replacing by $A_j$ by $A_{jp}$ does not increase the maximum $\phi$-value. For this same reason, we can infer that $\tilde{\mathcal A}\in S_2$ as well. However, the total weighted degree of $\tilde{\mathcal A}$ is smaller than that of $\mathcal A$, which contradicts the assumption that $\mathcal A\in S_3$. Therefore, each $A_i$ is connected.) Now, recall that the graph $G$ we are working on is assumed to be a tree, so we can make the $k$ connected subsets $A_1,\dots,A_k$ pairwise nonadjacent by removing a vertex in each of some $k-1$ subsets. (See Figure \ref{fig:pairwisenonadj}).
nodes.statement_short: Show the sets are connected (else a component improves the extremal choice), then remove $k-1$ vertices to make them nonadjacent.

nodes.name: Goal of Step 2
nodes.statement: We prove that there exists $v_1\in A_1,\dots,v_{k-1}\in A_{k-1}$ such that \[A_1\setminus\{v_1\},\dots,A_{k-1}\setminus\{v_{k-1}\},V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1})\] are pairwise nonadjacent in this step.
nodes.statement_short: Goal of Step 2

nodes.name: Each A_i is connected
nodes.statement: Indeed, since $\mathcal A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)\in S_3$, each $A_i$ is connected. (This is because otherwise, if some $A_j$ is not connected, then we write \[A_j=A_{j1}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm},\] where $A_{j1},\dots,A_{jm}$ are the $m$ connected components of $A_j$. Now, by Lemma \ref{lemma:basic-phi}, since \[E(A_{j1},A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm})=\varnothing,\] we have \[\min\{\phi(A_{j1}),\phi(A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm})\}\le\phi(A_j).\] If it happens that $\phi(A_{j1})>\phi(A_j)$, then we apply Lemma \ref{lemma:basic-phi} and the same procedure on \[A_{j2}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm}=A_{j2}\cup(A_{j3}\cup\dots\cup A_{jm}),\] and eventually we will obtain some $1\le p\le m$ such that $\phi(A_{jp})\le\phi(A_j)$. Now note that the subpartition \[\tilde{\mathcal A}=(A_1,\dots,A_{jp},\dots,A_k)\] is in $S_1$, since replacing by $A_j$ by $A_{jp}$ does not increase the maximum $\phi$-value. For this same reason, we can infer that $\tilde{\mathcal A}\in S_2$ as well. However, the total weighted degree of $\tilde{\mathcal A}$ is smaller than that of $\mathcal A$, which contradicts the assumption that $\mathcal A\in S_3$. Therefore, each $A_i$ is connected.)
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 1 a disconnected $A_j$ could be replaced by a component, contradicting minimal weight.

nodes.name: Remove one vertex in k-1 sets
nodes.statement: Now, recall that the graph $G$ we are working on is assumed to be a tree, so we can make the $k$ connected subsets $A_1,\dots,A_k$ pairwise nonadjacent by removing a vertex in each of some $k-1$ subsets. (See Figure \ref{fig:pairwisenonadj}).
nodes.statement_short: Remove one vertex in k-1 sets

nodes.name: Step 3: Cheeger constant of the complement equals h_k
nodes.statement_short: Show $h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))=h_k(G)$ by an upper bound and a two-case contradiction.

nodes.name: Upper bound via A_k
nodes.statement: Firstly, note that we have \[h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))\le h_k(G).\] Indeed, since \[A_k\subseteq V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}),\] we have \[h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))=\min_{C\subseteq V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1})}\phi(C)\le\phi(A_k)=h_k(G).\]
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound via A_k

nodes.name: Suppose strict inequality and replace A_k
nodes.statement: Next, for the sake of contradiction, we suppose that $h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))<h_k(G)$. Then, by the definition of $h$, there is some $A_k'\subseteq V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1})$ such that \[\phi(A_k')=h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))<h_k(G).\] Then, we can replace $A_k$ by $A_k'$ and consider the subpartition \[\mathcal A':=(A_1',\dots,A_{k-1}',A_k'):=(A_1,\dots,A_{k-1},A_k'),\] where $A_i':=A_i$ for $1\le i\le k-1$. We divide into two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Suppose strict inequality and replace A_k

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: \textsl{Case 1.} $\phi(A_{k-1})=\phi(A_k)=h_k(G)$. \newline Then, $f(\mathcal A')=f(\mathcal A)-1<f(\mathcal A)$ contradicts the assumption that $\mathcal A\in S_3\subseteq S_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 1

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: \textsl{Case 2.} $\phi(A_{k-1})<\phi(A_k)=h_k(G)$. \newline Then, \[\max_{1\le i\le k}\phi(A_i')=\max\{\phi(A_{k-1}),\phi(A_k')\}<h_k(G)\] contradicts the assumption that $\mathcal A\in S_3\subseteq S_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 2

nodes.name: Equality established
nodes.statement: Therefore, we must have $h(V\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{k-1}))=h_k(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality established

nodes.name: Step 4: pieces A_i minus v_i have Cheeger constant at least h_k
nodes.statement_short: A smaller subset of $A_j\setminus\{v_j\}$ with $\phi<h_k$ would give a lighter extremal subpartition.

nodes.name: Step 5: Dirichlet Cheeger constant at least h_k
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Step 6: sketch for forests
nodes.statement: \underline{Step 6. Sketch for the general case when $G$ is a weighted forest.} \newline\noindent We can actually apply the same idea as above. Namely, pick a subpartition from $S_3$ and remove $v_1\dots,v_{k-1}$ in order to achieve the pairwise nonadjacency. If there are some remaining quotas of the $k-1$ quotas, we can safely remove any vertices that are unrelated to the subgraph that achieves the minimum $\phi$-value.
nodes.statement_short: Same idea for forests, spending leftover vertex removals harmlessly.

nodes.name: Step 7: h_k at least l_k for every graph
nodes.statement: \underline{Step 7. Showing $h_k(\tilde G)\ge\ell_k(\tilde G)$ for any weighted graph $\tilde G=(\tilde V,\tilde E,\tilde\mu,\tilde w)$.} \newline\noindent It suffices to show that for any subpartitions $(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ and $(B_1,\dots,B_{n-k+1})$ of $\tilde V$, we have \[\max_{1\le i\le k}\phi(A_i)\ge\min_{B\in \mathcal{U}(B_1,\cdots,B_{n-k+1})}\phi(B).\] Let $|\tilde V|=n$, apply Lemma \ref{lem:pigeonhole} to take the desired common union $C$. Note that the induced subgraph is connected, so the minimum on the right side is attained by $C$, while the maximum on the left side is attained by some ``worst'' connected component of the induced subgraph of $C$, whose $\phi$-value must not be less than that of the induced subgraph.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the pigeonhole lemma to get a common union $C$ comparing max and min.

nodes.name: Step 8: conclusion
nodes.statement: \underline{Step 8. Conclusion.} \newline\noindent Since it is obvious that $\ell_k(\tilde G)\ge\underline{\ell_k}(\tilde G)$ for any weighted graph $\tilde G$, the proof is established.
nodes.statement_short: Step 8: conclusion

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: In fact, suppose the contrary, that $S\cap X=\varnothing$. Without loss of generality, we may assume $X=\mathbb{R}^{n-k+1}$. nodes.statement: Since the function $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\ni x\mapsto \Phi_1(x)$ is zero-homogeneous, any linear subspace $X$ can be replaced by its unit sphere $S:=X\cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ such that $\dim X=\mathrm{ind}(X\cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1})=\mathrm{ind}(S)$ with nothing changes, i.e., $$\min_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X=k}}~\max_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \Phi_1(x)=\min_{\substack{S=X\cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}\\\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max_{x\in S}\Phi_1(x) .$$ Replacing $\inf\limits_{S\in\mathcal{I}_k}~\sup\limits_{x\in S}\Phi_1(x)$ in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:general-graph-delta} by $\inf\limits_{\dim X=k}~\sup\limits_{x\in X}\Phi_1(x)$ yields the similar inequality \begin{align*}h_k(G)&\ge\min\limits_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max\limits_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|}\\&\ge \max\limits_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min\limits_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} \ge \ell_k(G) .\end{align*} Since $G$ is a forest, we can use the equality $h_k(G)=\ell_k(G)$ in Theorem \ref{thm:h_k=H_k} to derive the nonlinear Courant-Fischer-Weyl minimax equality.
nodes.statement_short: Replace subspaces by their unit spheres (zero-homogeneity), rerun Lemma 7's argument with subspaces, and close with $h_k=\ell_k$ on forests.

nodes.statement: Replacing $\inf\limits_{S\in\mathcal{I}_k}~\sup\limits_{x\in S}\Phi_1(x)$ in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:general-graph-delta} by $\inf\limits_{\dim X=k}~\sup\limits_{x\in X}\Phi_1(x)$ yields the similar inequality \begin{align*}h_k(G)&\ge\min\limits_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= k}}~\max\limits_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|}\\&\ge \max\limits_{\substack{\text{linear subspaces }X\text{ of }\mathbb R^n\\\dim X= n-k+1}}~\min\limits_{x\in X\setminus\{0\}} \frac{\sum\limits_{u\sim v}w_{uv}|x_u-x_v|}{\sum\limits_v\mu_v|x_v|} \ge \ell_k(G) .\end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3
nodes.statement: We can express the two monotonicity inequalities in Lemma \ref{lem:p-monotonicity} as $$ \swarrow\frac{1}{2^{p-1}}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le \lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le \frac p2 (2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}\nearrow $$ where the left-hand term $\frac p2 (2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}$ is increasing with respect to $p\in[1,+\infty)$, while the right-hand term $\frac{1}{2^{p-1}}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)$ is decreasing with respect to $p\in[1,+\infty)$. Substituting the equality $h_k(G)=\lambda_k(\Delta_1)$ into the above inequality immediately yields the conclusion of Corollary \ref{cor:tree-p-Lap}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:general-graph-delta}, $h_k(G)\ge \lambda_k(\Delta_1)\ge \ell_k(G)$ for any graph $G$ and any $k$. By Theorem \ref{thm:h_k=H_k}, we have $\ell_k(G)\ge \underline{\ell_k}(G)$, and according to Theorem \ref{thm:cycle-number-inequ}, we have $\underline{\ell_k}(G)\ge h_{k-\beta}(G)$. Thus, we finally obtain $\lambda_k(\Delta_1)\ge h_{k-\beta}(G)$, which completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:beta}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: To give a proof of Theorem \ref{thm:beta-p}, we require the monotonicity of $p$-Laplacian eigenvalues, see Lemma \ref{lem:p-monotonicity} in Section \ref{sec:tools}. In fact, we shall use the inequalities \[p(2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}\ge 2\lambda_k(\Delta_1)\text{ and }2^{-p}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le 2^{-1}\lambda_k(\Delta_1)\] in Lemma \ref{lem:p-monotonicity}. Combining these two inequalities with Theorem \ref{thm:beta}, we derive $$2^{1-p}\lambda_k(\Delta_p)\le \lambda_k(\Delta_1)\le h_k(G)$$ and $$p(2\lambda_k(\Delta_p))^{\frac1p}\ge 2\lambda_k(\Delta_1)\ge 2h_{k-\beta}(G).$$ This proves Theorem \ref{thm:beta-p}.
